chunks.title: The answer
chunks.text: Mandatory third party evaluation is preferred: the highest expected net social value among the alternatives that satisfy the constraints, and above the status quo. Mandatory third party evaluation: expected net social value $23.2bn (95% confidence interval $12.9bn to $35.0bn) over 5 years; simulated outcomes -$37.2bn to $78.3bn (10th to 90th percentile); harm avoided $14.2bn; industry value change -$41bn; within the constraints in 100% of resamples; best feasible alternative in 100% of resamples (ranking stability under the model, not the probability of being best in the world).

chunks.title: Constraints
chunks.text: Constraints: industry loss at most $300bn; P(catastrophe) at most 14%. Status quo (voluntary commitments): fails (industry loss $-0bn within the $300bn limit (satisfied in 100% of resamples); probability of a catastrophe 14.7% above the 14% ceiling (satisfied in 3% of resamples)). Mandatory third party evaluation: within (industry loss $41bn within the $300bn limit (satisfied in 100% of resamples); probability of a catastrophe 12.6% within the 14% ceiling (satisfied in 100% of resamples)). Strict liability: fails (industry loss $1,232bn exceeds the $300bn limit (satisfied in 0% of resamples); probability of a catastrophe 14.1% above the 14% ceiling (satisfied in 40% of resamples)). Liability with a safe harbour: fails (industry loss $371bn exceeds the $300bn limit (satisfied in 0% of resamples); probability of a catastrophe 12.0% within the 14% ceiling (satisfied in 100% of resamples)). Under the conservative rule (feasible in at least 90% of resamples) the preferred option is Mandatory third party evaluation.

chunks.title: Decision gap
chunks.text: Headline order Mandatory third party evaluation, Strict liability, Liability with a safe harbour; social order Liability with a safe harbour, Mandatory third party evaluation, Strict liability; Kendall tau b -0.33; decision gap 0.67; P(inversion) 100%. headline score: the value weighted price reaction against the status quo over the first six months plus a tenth of the early news tone difference; social order: expected net social value over the horizon; Kendall tau b, so tied scores do not create or hide a gap.

chunks.title: How sure, on these paths
chunks.text: 120 paths per alternative (schedule 120; ceiling 480), 500 bootstrap resamples. Three things are kept apart: the 95% confidence interval of an expected value (Monte Carlo error), the 10th to 90th percentile spread of simulated outcomes, and the range under alternative assumptions (the screen and the joint draw). Every precision target was met. In 4 independent batches of 30 paths the decision is the same in 3. Running estimate: 15 paths, decision Liability with a safe harbour, Mandatory third party evaluation $41.0bn (standard error 17.52); 30 paths, decision Liability with a safe harbour, Mandatory third party evaluation $30.5bn (standard error 10.20); 60 paths, decision Mandatory third party evaluation, Mandatory third party evaluation $30.7bn (standard error 9.43); 120 paths, decision Mandatory third party evaluation, Mandatory third party evaluation $23.2bn (standard error 5.56).

chunks.title: Screen of every assumption (tornado)
chunks.text: All 68 assumptions moved to the ends of their plausible ranges, the decision re made under each. Mandatory third party evaluation is worth $23.2bn at the run's values. Relocation cost: -$85.8bn at 0.04 and $23.2bn at 0.16, decision changes. Monthly catastrophe probability: $14.7bn at 0.0005 and $106.2bn at 0.005, decision changes. Audit rate: $11.5bn at 0.3 and -$63.5bn at 0.8, decision changes. Weight of safety culture: $52.8bn at 0.3 and -$18.0bn at 1.2, decision changes. Trust sensitivity to harm: -$6.8bn at 0.02 and $62.3bn at 0.08. Safety decay: -$24.6bn at 0.01 and $37.6bn at 0.04, decision changes. Capability growth: -$46.4bn at 0.015 and -$92.9bn at 0.035, decision changes. Safety spend that displaces capability R&D: -$2.9bn at 0.3 and $42.5bn at 1.0, decision changes. Trust elasticity of adoption benefits: $5.0bn at 0.2 and $48.4bn at 1.0. Reach ceiling saturation: -$9.8bn at 1.0 and $26.0bn at 2.2. Safety elasticity of incidents: $17.3bn at 1.4 and -$18.0bn at 3.0, decision changes. Output uplift base: $12.2bn at 200.0 and $45.0bn at 800.0. Revenue lost offshore: -$8.3bn at 0.06 and $23.2bn at 0.24. Median harm of a catastrophe: $16.0bn at 150.0 and $46.0bn at 1200.0, decision changes. Safety learning rate: $17.4bn at 0.05 and -$9.0bn at 0.12, decision changes. The decision changes at an end of the range of 18 of the 68 assumptions; those with the largest swings are Relocation cost, Monthly catastrophe probability, Audit rate, Weight of safety culture, Safety decay, Capability growth, Safety spend that displaces capability R&D, Safety elasticity of incidents, Median harm of a catastrophe, Safety learning rate, Revenue response to capability, Critical capability.

chunks.title: Joint draw of all the assumptions
chunks.text: 64 joint draws over the plausible ranges. The status quo: mean $0.0bn ($0.0bn to $0.0bn), the decision in 28% of draws, within the constraints and above the status quo in 44%, expected regret where it is within the constraints $22.8bn. Mandatory third party evaluation: mean -$16.7bn (-$175.9bn to $144.7bn), the decision in 19% of draws, within the constraints and above the status quo in 19%, expected regret where it is within the constraints $26.3bn. Liability with a safe harbour: mean $88.0bn (-$6.4bn to $284.0bn), the decision in 8% of draws, within the constraints and above the status quo in 8%, expected regret where it is within the constraints $0.0bn. Strict liability: mean $21.0bn (-$41.8bn to $117.5bn), the decision in 0% of draws, within the constraints and above the status quo in 0%, expected regret where it is within the constraints not defined (never within them). The decision margin moves with Relocation cost (rank correlation +0.48), Reach adjustment speed (rank correlation -0.38), Capability growth (rank correlation -0.37), the assumptions that pass a 10% false discovery rate over all 68. triangular distributions on the declared plausible ranges with the mode at the run's value, correlated groups joined by a Gaussian copula; a prior over the assumptions, not a posterior estimated from data.

chunks.title: Variance decomposition
chunks.text: Sobol indices over 5 assumptions for Mandatory third party evaluation, shares with interactions and their 90% intervals: Relocation cost: 46% of the value's variance (34% to 67%) and 46% of the margin's (32% to 65%). Audit rate: 34% of the value's variance (24% to 51%) and 34% of the margin's (25% to 50%). Weight of safety culture: 30% of the value's variance (11% to 54%) and 30% of the margin's (11% to 57%). Trust sensitivity to harm: 6% of the value's variance (4% to 9%) and 6% of the margin's (4% to 10%). Monthly catastrophe probability: 2% of the value's variance (1% to 3%) and 2% of the margin's (1% to 3%). The intervals are wide: the design ranks groups of assumptions and does not order neighbours. Saltelli's design on scrambled Sobol points; first order by Saltelli (2010), total order by Jansen (1999); 90% bootstrap intervals over the base sample; the other assumptions are held at the run's values, so the shares are of the variance these inputs produce, and the inputs are drawn independently, as the decomposition requires.

chunks.title: Structural variants
chunks.text: Mandatory third party evaluation remains the decision in 3 of 8 variants and stays within the constraints and above the status quo in 2. Myopic firms (firms plan six months ahead instead of twelve): decision Liability with a safe harbour, focus rank 3, outside the constraints. Forward looking firms (firms plan two years ahead): decision Mandatory third party evaluation, focus rank 3, within the constraints. Weak regulator (the regulator has half the stated capacity): decision none, focus rank 3, outside the constraints. Strong safety effect (safety practice cuts incidents faster): decision the status quo, focus rank 3, within the constraints. Weak safety effect (safety practice cuts incidents more slowly): decision none, focus rank 2, outside the constraints. Lax offshore (offshore activity is twice as hazardous as at home): decision Mandatory third party evaluation, focus rank 2, within the constraints. Heavy tail (the catastrophic tail is two and a half times more likely): decision none, focus rank 2, outside the constraints. Systemic catastrophes (catastrophic failures are strongly correlated across firms): decision Mandatory third party evaluation, focus rank 2, within the constraints.

chunks.title: Robustness
chunks.text: Robustly acceptable: no instrument (within the constraints and above the status quo on the central estimate, in at least 90% of the joint draws, in every structural variant and under every gaming strategy). Mandatory third party evaluation: central yes, joint draws 19%, structural 2 of 8, gaming no. Strict liability: central no, joint draws 0%, structural 0 of 8, gaming no. Liability with a safe harbour: central no, joint draws 8%, structural 1 of 8, gaming no.

chunks.title: Benchmarks: the model against published evidence
chunks.text: Annual growth of recorded AI incidents (direct): observed 56% (sd 26%), model 42%, not contradicted, across the declared ranges 31% to 67%. Annual change in public trust in AI and AI companies (direct): observed -5.1% (sd 2.3%), model -6.2%, not contradicted, across the declared ranges -16.5% to -2.2%. Share of a fall in trust recovered about nine months after a salient incident (analogue): observed 20% (sd 35%), model 37%, not contradicted, across the declared ranges 30% to 56%. Compliance cost of a high risk regime as a share of development spending in scope (official): observed 10.8% (sd 6.9%), model 12.1%, not contradicted, across the declared ranges 9.0% to 13.4%. Effect of a horizontal compliance regime on the profits of firms in scope (analogue): observed -3.3% (sd 3.9%), model -7.4%, not contradicted, across the declared ranges -9.7% to -5.9%. Equity return when a horizontal regime becomes enforceable (analogue): observed -0.9% (sd 1.0%), model -4.9%, contradicted; a failure of form, left out of the weights, across the declared ranges -5.6% to -3.3%. Equity return of a firm when a regulatory fine is announced (analogue): observed -0.7% (sd 1.0%), model -0.2%, not contradicted, across the declared ranges -0.8% to +0.8%. Equity return of a firm when a serious incident becomes public (analogue): observed -1.1% (sd 1.1%), model -1.2%, not contradicted, across the declared ranges -1.0% to +3.9%. Share of regulated activity displaced abroad by a unilateral regime (analogue): observed 14.0% (sd 8.6%), model 24.8%, not contradicted, across the declared ranges 0.3% to 25.2%. Premium above expected claims in liability insurance (analogue): observed 31% (sd 15%), model 25%, not contradicted, across the declared ranges 16% to 42%. Share of the insurance loading used up by underwriting and administration (analogue): observed 107% (sd 25%), model 50%, in tension, across the declared ranges 33% to 66%. Sources: Annual growth of recorded AI incidents: Stanford HAI, AI Index Report 2025, chapter 3 (233 incidents in 2024, up 56.4% on 2023); Stanford HAI, AI Index Report 2026, responsible AI (362 incidents in 2025). Annual change in public trust in AI and AI companies: Edelman Trust Barometer 2024, key insights around AI; Pew Research Center, How Americans view AI and its impact on people and society, September 2025. Share of a fall in trust recovered about nine months after a salient incident: AAA, Three in four Americans remain afraid of fully self driving vehicles, March 2019; Smart Cities Dive, AAA poll, March 2019 (the 2018 figure and the crashes). Compliance cost of a high risk regime as a share of development spending in scope: European Commission, SWD(2021) 84 final, impact assessment of the AI Act; Renda et al. (2021), Study to support an impact assessment of regulatory requirements for AI in Europe. Effect of a horizontal compliance regime on the profits of firms in scope: Chen, Frey and Presidente (2022), Privacy regulation and firm performance, Oxford Martin working paper 2022-1; Johnson (2022), Economic research on privacy regulation: lessons from the GDPR and beyond, NBER working paper 30705. Equity return when a horizontal regime becomes enforceable: Motoki and Pinto (2024), Journal of Business Finance and Accounting (press summary). Equity return of a firm when a regulatory fine is announced: Ford et al. (2021), The impact of GDPR infringement fines on the market value of firms, ECCWS. Equity return of a firm when a serious incident becomes public: Kamiya, Kang, Kim, Milidonis and Stulz, What is the impact of successful cyberattacks on target firms? (authors' summary, Harvard Law School Forum on Corporate Governance, March 2018; Journal of Financial Economics 139(3), 2021). Share of regulated activity displaced abroad by a unilateral regime: Branger and Quirion (2014), Ecological Economics 99. Premium above expected claims in liability insurance: NAIC, U.S. property and casualty and title insurance industries, 2023 full year results. Share of the insurance loading used up by underwriting and administration: NAIC, U.S. property and casualty and title insurance industries, 2023 full year results.

chunks.title: Evidence examined and set aside
chunks.text: Meta analysis of trust and intention to use a technology: r = 0.503 (95% interval 0.470 to 0.535, 128 samples, 50,667 respondents): not used because it supports the sign of the trust channel and nothing more: a correlation between stated attitudes in studies of online shopping, banking and e-health is not an elasticity of realised adoption to trust, and cannot be turned into one without the dispersion of both. The elasticity stays unidentified. The size of the fall in trust after a salient incident (AAA: afraid to ride rose from 63% to 73% after two fatal crashes): not used because the model moves trust with monetised harm, and two deaths are a small monetised harm: an incident of that size moves the model's trust by less than a tenth of a percent. The episode says trust answers to salience; the model's form cannot show that. Recorded as a limit of the mechanism, not scored, because the survey question is about using a vehicle. Estimates of AI's effect on output: total factor productivity up by no more than 0.66% over ten years (Acemoglu); 7% of global GDP over ten years (Goldman Sachs); $2.6 to $4.4 trillion a year (McKinsey): not used because the model declares its benefit bases in $bn a year and declares no size for the jurisdiction's economy, so there is nothing to divide by; and the estimates span an order of magnitude. Elicited probabilities of catastrophic harm from AI: not used because elicitations, not observations; they define catastrophe differently from the model and have no validation record. A loss distribution for AI incidents: not used because none has been published: the taxonomies exist, the magnitudes are not recorded. GDPR and venture investment: monthly EU deals down 26.1% against US ventures: not used because the model has no entry or investment margin to compare it with.

chunks.title: Validation and evidence
chunks.text: The Lab is synthetic: its figures are conditional on the model and its assumptions and are not validated forecasts. The model was confronted with 11 published benchmarks that bear on 10 of its 15 mechanisms. 3 of those mechanisms have a benchmark measured on AI itself; the others rest on analogues from other regulation and other technologies, each compared with an allowance for that distance. At the central assumptions the model is not contradicted by 9, is in tension with 1 (Share of the insurance loading used up by underwriting and administration) and is contradicted by 1 (Equity return when a horizontal regime becomes enforceable). Even the closest tenth of the draws of the assumptions miss Equity return when a horizontal regime becomes enforceable by more than 2 standard deviations: that is a failure of the model's form and not of a parameter value, so it is reported and left out of the weighting below. No benchmark bears on 5 mechanisms: severity, catastrophic tail, safety practice, evaluation, news. Weighting the 64 joint draws of the assumptions by how well each reproduces the 10 benchmarks it can be compared with leaves an effective 13 draws. In the weighted draws the decision is no alternative in 45% (unweighted 45%); the status quo in 23% (unweighted 28%); Mandatory third party evaluation in 20% (unweighted 19%); Liability with a safe harbour in 12% (unweighted 8%). 80% of the draws are ruled out by no benchmark at 3 standard deviations. Mandatory third party evaluation is within the constraints and above the status quo in 27% of the weighted draws (19% unweighted). Fewer than 20 effective draws: the weighted shares are indicative only on this budget. The benchmarks bear on 13 of the 68 assumptions drawn; they move most Resource share of the insurance loading (+0.7 sd), Capability elasticity of incidents (-0.3 sd), Weight firms put on growth (-0.2 sd), Revenue lost offshore (-0.2 sd), Relocation cost (-0.2 sd). Weighting by benchmarks is a posterior given the allowances declared for each benchmark, not a measurement: most of the evidence is an analogue, and a wide allowance makes a benchmark easy to pass and uninformative. What the benchmarks do not reach is listed with the reasons; in particular nothing here identifies the elasticity of realised adoption to trust. No price series of an observed event was uploaded on this run. No mechanism is estimated from data; 10 of 15 were confronted with a published benchmark.

chunks.title: Mechanism register
chunks.text: Reportable incidents arrive at a rate that rises with released capability and deployment reach and falls with safety practice: uncalibrated; test: Held out incident counts per firm and year inside the model's predictive interval; the sign and size of the safety elasticity from before and after comparisons at firms that adopt evaluation regimes. The monetised harm of an incident is lognormal with a heavy tail; an incident at or above a threshold is major: uncalibrated; test: The empirical tail of documented losses against the lognormal fit; the share of incidents above the major threshold. Above a critical capability a firm faces a small monthly probability of a catastrophic incident, reduced by safety practice and evaluation, and correlated across firms: uncalibrated, untestable ex ante; test: Not testable before the event. Treated by sensitivity: both ends of every range in the screen, the joint draw, and the heavy tail and systemic variants. Near miss frequencies would be partial evidence on the prior. The share of R&D spent on safety raises safety practice with diminishing returns and displaces part of capability growth; practice decays without investment: uncalibrated; test: Firm level safety budgets against evaluation pass rates and incident rates over time. A mandated evaluation catches a share of unsafe releases before deployment: uncalibrated; test: Post mortems of incidents: the share traceable to failures an evaluation at release would have found. Each month a firm chooses its safety share, offshore share and whether to comply by maximising a one year expected payoff under its own optimistic view of incident risk: uncalibrated; test: Observed compliance rates, safety budgets and release cadence after an instrument takes effect, against the model's. Firms move activity offshore when the instrument binds at home; moved activity is laxer, loses revenue and takes domestic rents with it: uncalibrated; test: Changes in establishment location, hiring and model release geography around regulatory dates, against unaffected sectors. Capability grows with R&D; licensing delays releases; a moratorium freezes released capability and slows research in scope; published weights diffuse capability: uncalibrated; test: Release cadence and benchmark trajectories before and after a licensing regime. Reach closes on a ceiling set by released capability and public trust; trust falls with harm and recovers slowly; adoption benefits scale with trust: uncalibrated; test: Survey trust and adoption series around salient incidents. A firm's revenue grows at a rate that fades from its starting pace towards a long run rate, moves with released capability and reach, and for chip and cloud firms with the developers' growth: uncalibrated; test: Revenue growth of listed AI firms against capability releases and adoption series. Enforcement intensity follows news pressure within the regulator's capacity; audits find the non compliant and fine them: uncalibrated; test: Enforcement actions against news attention series for an existing regulator. Incidents, enforcement, relocations and releases become a news pressure index with memory, and a wire of headlines on the representative path: uncalibrated; test: Forecast coverage counts for a policy domain against observed counts. A firm's price is a fundamental value (revenue and forward earnings multiples) times a sentiment component driven by the market factor, news pressure, incident jumps and, for an instrument announced before it takes effect, an anticipation term: partly calibrable; one mechanism testable here; test: Implemented: an event study on an uploaded series mapped to a firm and an instrument, against the model's predictive distribution of the early reaction; with eight or more mapped events, the coverage of the 10th to 90th percentile band. Consumer surplus and the output uplift are powers of the AI service index around declared annual bases: declared value judgements; test: Not a testable mechanism: a valuation. Treated by sensitivity. Liability moves a share of harm to the firm in scope; a safe harbour shields the compliant; a mandate replaces realised liability with a premium loaded above expected claims: uncalibrated; test: Quoted premiums and exclusions for AI liability cover against the model's.

chunks.title: Assumptions
chunks.text: Social discount rate 0.03 a year (social discount rate applied to every monthly flow). Harm valuation multiplier 1.0 multiple (scales the monetised harm of incidents; 1.0 takes the engine's damages at face value). Consumer surplus base 250.0 $bn a year (annual consumer surplus from AI services at the starting level of capability and reach). Consumer surplus elasticity 0.6 elasticity (proportional change in consumer surplus per proportional change in the AI service index). Output uplift base 400.0 $bn a year (annual output uplift attributable to AI adoption at the starting service index). Output uplift elasticity 0.8 elasticity (proportional change in the output uplift per proportional change in the service index). Trust elasticity of adoption benefits 0.5 elasticity (proportional change in realised adoption benefits per proportional change in public trust). Overlap of the output uplift with other benefits 0.0 share (share of the output uplift already counted as consumer surplus or as the AI firms' own profit, removed from the output uplift; 0 takes the three benefit components as defined, without overlap). chunks.title: Instruments
chunks.text: Status quo (voluntary commitments): No new obligation. Existing consumer and product law only, with the regulator's present capacity. Every other policy is measured against this path, pair by pair. Liability with a safe harbour: Strict liability, but a firm that meets the evaluation and safety spend standard is shielded from most of it. Compliance becomes the cheaper choice. Mandatory third party evaluation: Independent pre deployment evaluation above a threshold, with a short approval delay. Catches a share of unsafe releases before they ship. Strict liability: Firms pay for the harm their systems cause, insured by mandate. No ex ante obligation: the price of an incident does the work, and the firms choose their own safety spend.
